title: 15 places in New Jersey to take the grandkids
dek: Zoos, aquariums, farms and a battleship, chosen for children and grandparents alike. Here is where the benches, elevators and wheelchair rentals are, and what seniors pay.
keyFacts: Cape May County Park & Zoo charges nothing for admission or car parking.
Duke Farms and Howell Living History Farm are free. The New Jersey State Museum is free, with $10 planetarium shows.
Bergen County Zoo charges seniors 62+ just $2 (county residents) or $4.
Adventure Aquarium rents manual wheelchairs for $8 and scooters for $30, plus refundable deposits.
Space Farms Zoo & Museum closes for the 2026 season on November 1.
body:
A day out with the grandkids works best when it works for everyone. Little legs need a playground and a snack. Older knees need a bench, a level path and a restroom that is not a half mile away. New Jersey has plenty of places that manage both.

We checked the places below on their official websites in October 2026. We list prices only where the site posts them, and we say so when it does not. Hours shift a lot between fall and winter, and some spots close for the season, so call before you load the car.

Plan the day around the slowest walker and the youngest napper, and everyone has a better time.

How do I plan a day that works for both of us?

  1. Pick one main stop. Two attractions in one day sounds fun and usually ends in tears, some of them yours. Leave time for lunch and a sit-down.
  2. Look up the map before you go. Find the restrooms, the café, the elevators and the closest parking to the entrance. Many sites post an accessibility page.
  3. Ask about wheelchairs and strollers. Several places below lend or rent them, usually first come, first served. A rented wheelchair can turn a two-hour visit into a four-hour one.
  4. Go early on a weekday if you can. School-day mornings are quieter for toddlers and preschoolers, and parking is easier.
  5. Pack for two generations. Bring your medications, water, snacks, a change of clothes for the child and a charged phone. Write your cell number on a card in the child's pocket.
  6. Ask about senior rates. Many places discount for 62+ or 65+. Bring ID.

North Jersey: where should we go?

1. Turtle Back Zoo, West Orange

Essex County's zoo is compact and busy, with a train, a carousel and a touch tank. The zoo says plainly that it is built on a mountain and has steep paths, with benches throughout for breaks. A limited number of wheelchairs and strollers can be rented at Guest Relations, first come, first served, and the train is wheelchair accessible. Stroller rentals close for winter. Parking in the South Mountain Recreation Complex is free. The zoo sells a senior ticket for visitors 62 and older. Call 973-731-5800 ext. 0 for current rates.

2. Bergen County Zoo, Paramus

This small zoo inside Van Saun County Park is easy to cover in a morning, which makes it a good first zoo. Standard hours are 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., last entry at 4. Bergen County residents 62 and older pay $2 and out-of-county seniors pay $4. Children 3 to 14 pay $4 (residents) or $7, and children under 3 are free. The train and carousel cost $3 per person, per ride, sold only at the zoo booth. Questions: 201-634-3100.

3. Liberty Science Center, Jersey City

Four floors of hands-on science, plus a planetarium, all indoors. That makes it a strong pick for a cold or rainy day. Each floor has two large elevators, and a third serves the planetarium. Wheelchairs can be requested at the Welcome Desk. There is a drop-off area near the entrance for guests with special needs, reached from Phillip Street. Parking costs $7 for cars. The center is closed some weekdays, so check the schedule. Prices are posted only through the online ticket system, and buying a day ahead gets the best price. Call 201-200-1000.

4. Paterson Great Falls, Paterson

Kids love the roar. The Passaic River drops about 77 feet between dark cliffs, and the view from the overlook railing is free. It is a short visit, which suits a child with a short attention span. Overlook Park has accessible parking, but paths mix paved and unpaved sections. There are no restrooms in the park. Accessible restrooms are at the Paterson Museum, 2 Market Street. Park office: 973-523-0370.

5. Silas Condict County Park, Kinnelon

A quiet nature outing for grandkids who like to throw sticks in water and look for ducks. The park covers 1,513 acres with more than 10 miles of trails. The easy part is the seven-acre lake, which has benches and is partly lined with weeping cherry trees. There are picnic sites with tables and grills. It is open sunrise to sunset. The county page does not describe accessibility, so call 973-326-7600 before bringing a wheelchair.

6. Space Farms Zoo & Museum, Wantage

Part zoo, part old-time museum. More than 500 animals share the grounds with nine museum buildings holding over 50 antique cars, carriages, dolls and farm machines. Grandparents often enjoy the museum as much as the kids enjoy the bears. There is a picnic area, a playground and a pizza restaurant. The 2026 season ends Sunday, November 1, so go soon or plan for spring. Hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., last entrance 4 p.m. Daily tickets start at $26. The site does not post a senior rate or accessibility details. Call 973-875-3223.

Central Jersey: what is worth the drive?

7. Duke Farms, Hillsborough

Doris Duke's former estate is now 2,700 acres of meadows, woods and ponds, and entry is always free. More than 15 miles of trails are mostly flat, paved and wider than 36 inches, which is great for strollers and wheelchairs. The Orchid Range is a mile from the Farm Barn and cannot be reached by car. Duke Farms offers a free round-trip accessibility transport there for people with limited mobility, by reservation. There are benches along the path to the Farm Barn. The campus is closed every Sunday and Monday. Saturdays from April through October need a free parking pass.

8. Grounds For Sculpture, Hamilton

Giant outdoor sculptures hide around every bend, which turns a walk into a treasure hunt. The main path is paved, though side paths can be gravel, sand or steep. Wheelchairs rent for $15 a day and scooters for $29 for the first four hours. Seniors 65 and older pay $18 (adults $25). Timed tickets must be booked online in advance. Closed Tuesdays.

9. New Jersey State Museum and Planetarium, Trenton

Dinosaurs, fossils and Native American history, next to the State House. General admission is free. Planetarium shows cost $10, with $1 off for seniors 65 and older. Use the Planetarium entrance if walking is hard. Every level has two elevators, most galleries have benches, and the front desk lends one free wheelchair. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

10. Howell Living History Farm, Hopewell Township

A working farm run as it was around 1900, with horses, plowing and real chores. Kids can often lend a hand. Admission and parking are free (the corn maze has a fee). It is open Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and closed Sundays, Mondays and Mercer County holidays. The Visitor Center is fully accessible, and transportation to the barnyard and fields is available on request. Picnicking is not allowed, so plan lunch elsewhere. Call 609-737-3299.

11. Jenkinson's Aquarium, Point Pleasant Beach

A manageable, indoor aquarium right on the boardwalk, with penguins, seals and sharks. Seniors 65 and older pay $15, adults $19 and children 3 to 11 pay $13. Children 2 and under are free. Fall and winter hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, closed Thanksgiving and Christmas. The wheelchair lift is being replaced and is out of service until about October 31, so call 732-892-0600 if anyone in your group needs it.

South Jersey: where can we spend a whole day?

12. Adventure Aquarium, Camden

Big and dramatic, with a shark bridge, hippos and penguins. The average visit runs two to three hours. General admission starts at $32.99 for adults and $27.99 for children, and seniors save $2. Manual wheelchairs rent for $8 (plus a $10 refundable deposit) and electric scooters for $30 (plus $50). Single strollers rent for $8. You may bring outside food. Parking is $10. The aquarium is mostly cashless. It is open 364 days a year, closed Thanksgiving. Call 1-844-474-3474.

13. Battleship New Jersey, Camden

A real Iowa-class battleship, docked across from Philadelphia. School-age kids tend to love it. It is full of steep ladders, but wheelchair users can reach the main deck exterior and the officers' wardroom using elevators, and there is a main deck tour of about 45 minutes that skips the ladders. A senior rate is not posted, so ask. To arrange accessible parking, call 1-866-877-6262 ext. 108.

14. Storybook Land, Egg Harbor Township

A gentle amusement park built around nursery rhymes, sized for small children. Seniors pay $39.95 online or at the door. Other visitors 2 to 64 pay $42.95 online or $45.95 at the gate, and children under 2 are free. In mid-October the park runs Friday hours plus special ticketed weekends, then switches to its Christmas Fantasy with Lights season. Holiday tickets go on sale online only starting October 28. An Assisted Access Pass at Guest Services helps guests who struggle with lines. Call 609-646-0103.

15. Cape May County Park & Zoo, Cape May Court House

One of the best deals in the state. Admission and car parking are free, and the zoo is open every day except Christmas. Zoo hours are 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. in summer and 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. in winter, and the park opens at 7 a.m. Strollers, wheelchairs and motorized scooters are available to rent. Two playgrounds sit just outside the zoo entrance. Outside food is allowed in the park but not inside the zoo, so plan a picnic before or after.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Trying to see everything. Pick the three animals or exhibits the child cares about most. Anything else is a bonus.
  • Skipping the rental. If you get tired after an hour of walking, rent the wheelchair or scooter. The child can ride along for a stretch, and you will both last longer.
  • Forgetting seasonal closures. Space Farms closes for the year on November 1, Duke Farms is closed Sundays and Mondays, and Grounds For Sculpture is closed Tuesdays.
  • Not bringing paperwork. If a parent is not along, carry a signed note with their phone number, the child's allergies and the pediatrician's name.

For more places to go, see our guides to day trips and free and discounted outings. If you are 62 or older, the free NJ Senior Citizen Pass also gets you into state parks without paying the entrance fee.

faq.q: Which of these places are free?
faq.a: Cape May County Park & Zoo, Duke Farms, Howell Living History Farm, the New Jersey State Museum (planetarium shows are extra) and the Paterson Great Falls overlook charge no admission. Silas Condict County Park is also free to visit.

faq.q: Where can I rent a wheelchair or scooter?
faq.a: Adventure Aquarium, Grounds For Sculpture and Cape May County Park & Zoo rent them. Turtle Back Zoo has a limited number for rent, and Liberty Science Center and the New Jersey State Museum have wheelchairs at the front desk. Supplies are small, so arrive early or call ahead.

faq.q: What is a good indoor choice for a cold or rainy day?
faq.a: Liberty Science Center, Adventure Aquarium, Jenkinson's Aquarium and the New Jersey State Museum are mostly or fully indoors. Check hours first, since Liberty Science Center closes on some weekdays.

faq.q: Do I need a note from the parents to take my grandchild out?
faq.a: It is smart to carry one. A signed note with the parents' phone numbers, the child's allergies and the pediatrician's name helps if there is an emergency or a medical visit.

title: How to stay active and social through a New Jersey winter
dek: Indoor walking spots, the gym benefit hiding in your Medicare plan, warming centers and the real risks of shoveling. A practical plan for the cold months.
keyFacts: Cherry Hill Mall opens at 9 a.m. daily for walkers. Bridgewater Commons walkers can start at 6:30 a.m. Monday to Saturday.
SilverSneakers and Renew Active come with many Medicare Advantage plans at no extra cost. Original Medicare does not cover gyms.
A Code Blue is declared at 32 degrees or below, or a wind chill of zero or below for two hours. Check nj211.org/njcodeblue.
The Winter Termination Program protects eligible households from utility shutoffs November 15 to March 15.
Driving with snow on your car can cost $25 to $75, or $200 to $1,000 if it causes injury or damage.
body:
A New Jersey winter can shrink your world fast. A week of ice, an early sunset and a car that stays in the driveway can leave you inside more than is good for body or mood. The fix is a plan made now, while the roads are still clear.

This guide covers where to walk indoors, how to use the fitness benefit that may already come with your Medicare plan, where to find company on gray afternoons, and how to stay safe when the cold turns serious. We checked every detail against official sources in October 2026.

The best time to plan for February is a sunny afternoon in October.

Where can I walk indoors when it is icy?

Malls have long doubled as winter walking tracks. They are flat, heated and lit, and there are benches and restrooms every few hundred feet. Several New Jersey malls officially welcome walkers before stores open:

  • Cherry Hill Mall opens early every morning for mall walkers. Doors open at 9 a.m., seven days a week.
  • Moorestown Mall welcomes walkers one hour before posted shopping hours each day.
  • Bridgewater Commons hosts HealthHike, a free walking program run with RWJ University Hospital Somerset. Walkers can start as early as 6:30 a.m. Monday through Saturday and at 9 a.m. Sunday. Sign up at the mall management office on weekdays to get an ID badge and a mileage card. Monthly meetings with health speakers run October through June. Call 908-595-2345.

Mall hours change, so confirm on the mall's website before you go. If no mall near you has a program, ask your town's recreation department or senior center. Some community centers and schools open gyms or tracks to residents in winter. Your local YMCA is another option, and many Ys take the Medicare fitness benefits described below.

Does my Medicare plan pay for a gym?

Original Medicare does not cover gym memberships. Many Medicare Advantage plans, and some Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plans, include a fitness program at no extra cost. The two you will hear about most are SilverSneakers and Renew Active.

SilverSneakers

SilverSneakers is offered through select Medicare Advantage and Medicare Supplement plans. Your eligibility depends on your plan, not your income. Here is how it works:

  1. Check eligibility. Use the SilverSneakers eligibility checker with the name and member ID exactly as they appear on your insurance card.
  2. Get your member ID. Create an account at SilverSneakers.com and download or print your SilverSneakers ID.
  3. Pick a location. Use the location finder to see partner gyms near you.
  4. Show your ID at the front desk. That is it. Classes held at community centers and parks, plus live and on-demand online classes, are included too.

Renew Active

Renew Active comes only with UnitedHealthcare Medicare plans. It includes a standard gym membership at participating locations at no additional cost, plus online classes and brain-health content. The gym network varies by plan and area, and not every plan includes it. Questions: 1-855-604-1588 (TTY 711).

Shopping for a plan right now?

Medicare open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. If a fitness benefit matters to you, check each plan's Evidence of Coverage before you switch. For free, unbiased help comparing plans, call New Jersey's SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820. Our guide to Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap explains the trade-offs.

Where can I find company on long winter days?

Your public library is often the warmest, friendliest building in town. Most New Jersey libraries run free book clubs, movie afternoons, technology help, craft groups and lectures through the winter. Many county library systems post their calendars online, and staff will gladly read the schedule to you over the phone.

Senior centers are the other anchor. Expect exercise classes, cards, lunch programs and day trips. Some arrange rides for members. To find the center nearest you, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 or dial 2-1-1.

Holiday light shows and seasonal events help break up December. Parks, zoos and botanical gardens around the state run evening light displays, and many towns hold tree lightings and holiday markets. Storybook Land in Egg Harbor Township, for example, runs its Christmas Fantasy with Lights season, with tickets sold online only starting October 28. Check each event's website for dates, as schedules are often set late in the fall. Weeknights tend to be less crowded, and some displays can be seen from a car.

What is a Code Blue, and where can I go to get warm?

Under New Jersey law, a county declares a Code Blue when temperatures will reach 32 degrees Fahrenheit or lower, or when the National Weather Service wind chill will be zero or below for at least two hours. During a Code Blue, counties open warming centers. These are mainly for people without shelter, but anyone who loses heat at home can ask for help.

  • Check current activations and warming centers by county at nj211.org/njcodeblue.
  • Call 2-1-1 or the Statewide Homeless Hotline at 1-877-652-1148 after hours.
  • Many public libraries, shopping centers and senior centers serve as warming spots during business hours.

Staying safe in the cold

Aging makes it harder to notice when your body is getting too cold. The National Institute on Aging advises setting your heat to at least 68 degrees, since even a home at 60 to 65 degrees can lead to hypothermia in older adults. Wear layers indoors, close the curtains at night and limit alcohol.

Know the warning signs of hypothermia: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness. Hypothermia is a medical emergency. Call 9-1-1.

Behind on the heating bill?

New Jersey's Winter Termination Program protects eligible households from utility shutoffs from November 15 through March 15. You may qualify if you receive PAAD, Lifeline, the Universal Service Fund, home energy assistance (LIHEAP) or SSI, or if you cannot pay because of illness, medical bills, job loss or a death in the family. LIHEAP applications are open October 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. See our guide to food and utility help.

Should I still shovel snow?

Think hard before you pick up the shovel. The American Heart Association warns that shoveling heavy snow can raise the risk of a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest. It is mostly arm work, which strains the heart more than leg work. People often hold their breath while lifting, and cold air tightens blood vessels.

The AHA's advice is direct. If you have heart disease or risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking or a past heart attack or stroke, have someone else clear the snow. If you must do it yourself:

  • Start slowly and take breaks.
  • Push or sweep snow rather than lifting and throwing it. Use a snow blower if you have one.
  • Cover your nose and mouth and dress in layers, with a hat and gloves.
  • Stop right away if you feel chest pain or pressure, lightheadedness or a racing or irregular heartbeat. Call 9-1-1 if it does not ease quickly.

Line up help before the first storm. A neighbor's teenager, a local landscaper or a church volunteer group can be booked in advance. Keep a bag of ice melt or sand by the door, and wear rubber-soled, low-heeled boots.

How do I handle winter driving, or not driving at all?

New Jersey law requires you to clear all snow and ice from your vehicle, including the hood, windows and roof, before you drive. Fines run $25 to $75 per offense, even if nothing flies off. If flying ice or snow causes injury or property damage, fines rise to $200 to $1,000.

The state's winter driving advice:

  • Drive at or below the speed limit and leave 8 to 10 seconds behind the car ahead.
  • Give snowplows plenty of room and avoid passing them.
  • If you skid, take your foot off the gas and gently steer in the direction the rear of the car is sliding.
  • Keep a kit in the car: ice scraper, blanket, flashlight, phone charger, water and snacks.
  • Check road conditions at 511nj.org before you leave.

Winter is also a natural time to think about cutting back. Many people stop driving at night or in bad weather first. Our guide to driving later in life covers how to make that call and what transportation options exist. NJ Transit offers reduced fares for riders 62 and older, and county transportation services can help with medical trips and errands.

When you cannot get out, keep in touch on purpose. Set up a daily check-in call with a friend or relative, join a phone or video group through your library or senior center, and arrange grocery and prescription delivery before a storm hits. See our guide to staying connected for more ideas.

faq.q: Does Original Medicare pay for SilverSneakers?
faq.a: No. SilverSneakers comes through select Medicare Advantage and Medicare Supplement plans. Renew Active comes only with UnitedHealthcare Medicare plans. Check your plan's Evidence of Coverage or call SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 for help comparing plans.

faq.q: How do I find a warming center near me?
faq.a: Visit nj211.org/njcodeblue to see which counties have a Code Blue in effect and where warming centers are open. You can also dial 2-1-1 or call 1-877-652-1148. Libraries and senior centers often serve as warm places during business hours.

faq.q: What temperature should I keep my home in winter?
faq.a: The National Institute on Aging recommends at least 68 degrees. Even a home kept at 60 to 65 degrees can lead to hypothermia in older adults.

faq.q: Is it safe for me to shovel snow?
faq.a: The American Heart Association advises people with heart disease or risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes or a past heart attack to have someone else do it. If you shovel, go slowly, push rather than lift, and stop if you feel chest pain or lightheaded.

faq.q: Can my utility shut off my heat in winter?
faq.a: If you qualify for the Winter Termination Program, your service cannot be cut off from November 15 through March 15. Recipients of PAAD, Lifeline, USF, LIHEAP and SSI qualify, as do people facing hardship such as illness or job loss. Contact your utility to enroll.
